n: Chapters 21–24 form an appendix of events from various times in David’s reign. A three-year famine strikes, and when David seeks the Lord, he learns it is because Saul broke Israel’s covenant with the Gibeonites by killing them.

f.g: A family guilty of shedding innocent blood.

n: The narrator explains: the Gibeonites were not Israelites but survivors of the Amorites, protected by an oath Israel made in Joshua’s day. Saul, in misguided zeal, tried to wipe them out.

f.w: the children of Israel had sworn unto them

f.g: A general name for the pre-Israelite peoples of Canaan.

n: David asks the Gibeonites what he can do to make amends so that they will bless the land instead of having cause to curse it.

f.g: Here, making things right — repairing a broken covenant.

n: They refuse money and do not claim the right to kill just any Israelite. David promises to do whatever they ask.

f.w: We will have no silver nor gold

n: They identify Saul as the man who tried to exterminate them from all Israel’s territory.
They ask for seven of Saul’s descendants to be executed at Saul’s hometown. It reflects the ancient view of collective family guilt — a harsh custom that later scripture moved away from.

f.w: hang them up unto the LORD
f.g: The Hebrew suggests executing and exposing the bodies, perhaps by impaling or dismembering.

n: David protects Mephibosheth, honoring his sacred oath to Jonathan. Here two covenants are kept: Israel’s with Gibeon and David’s with Jonathan.

f.w: the LORD's oath that was between them

n: He hands over two sons of Saul’s concubine Rizpah and five grandsons through Saul’s daughter. Most manuscripts say Michal, but the woman married to Adriel was her sister Merab, so many translations read Merab.

f.g: Merab, Michal’s older sister, was married to Adriel; a copyist may have confused the names.

n: The seven are executed together at Gibeah at the start of barley harvest, in early spring.

f.g: Around April, the first harvest of the year.

n: Rizpah, a grieving mother, spreads sackcloth on the rock and keeps vigil over the bodies for months, driving away birds and wild animals until the rains come. Her quiet, faithful love is one of the most moving scenes in the book.

f.w: until water dropped upon them out of heaven
f.g: Until the autumn rains — possibly a signal that the famine had ended.

n: David hears what Rizpah has done.
Moved by her devotion, David retrieves the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead, whose men had rescued them from the Philistines.

f.w: stolen them from the street of Beth-shan

n: He gathers their bones along with those of the seven who were executed.
They are all buried with honor in Saul’s family tomb in Benjamin. After this, God answers prayer for the land. Covenant faithfulness and respect for the dead bring healing.

f.w: the sepulchre of Kish his father
God was entreated for the land
f.g: God responded to prayers and ended the famine.

n: Several accounts of battles with Philistine giants follow. In one, David grows exhausted in battle.
A giant named Ishbi-benob, armed with a huge bronze spearhead and a new sword, tries to kill the tired David.

f.g: Possibly descendants of Rapha, ancestor of the giant Rephaim, or members of an elite warrior group.
About 7.5 pounds (3.4 kg) — half the weight of Goliath’s spearhead (1 Samuel 17:7).

n: Abishai rescues David. His men swear David must never again go to battle, lest Israel’s “lamp” be extinguished.

f.g: The king was the lamp of the nation; his life kept the people’s hope burning.

n: In another battle at Gob, Sibbechai kills another giant named Saph.

f.g: An unidentified place, perhaps near Gezer (1 Chronicles 20:4).

n: Elhanan kills Goliath’s brother, who carried a spear as thick as a weaver’s beam. The words “the brother of” are added by the translators; 1 Chronicles explains he killed Lahmi, Goliath’s brother.

f.g: The thick wooden rod on a loom.

n: At Gath, a giant with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot appears.
When he taunts Israel, as Goliath once did, David’s nephew Jonathan kills him.
These four giants of Gath were defeated by David and his men. David’s early victory over Goliath finds its echo in the victories of those he trained.
